Great Entrance and anaphora

Worship and practice · Divine Liturgy

Great Entrance and anaphora

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

The Great Entrance and the anaphora belong to the movement toward Eucharistic consecration. The gifts are the bread and wine offered, and anaphora names the Eucharistic prayer of offering and thanksgiving.[1][2]

What is the Great Entrance?[1]

Hapgood describes the Great Entrance as the transfer of the gifts from the place of preparation to the altar. Her commentary relates the procession to Christ’s Passion and distinguishes this moment from the later consecration. Its account of commemorations and historical customs remains attributed to that edition.[1]

Read original passage

Great Entrance

(17) In the middle of the Cherubimic Hymn the Great Entrance is made: that is to say, the Holy Gifts are brought from the Chapel (or Table) of Oblation to the Altar. In the days of the early Church, during this Great Entrance, all persons who had brought or sent offerings for the use of the Church were mentioned by name. But as this detailed commemoration was extremely long and difficult, it was ordered that only the chief personages in rank and power should thereafter be mentioned by name; all others being included under the honourable title of "all Orthodox Christians." If it be a Pontifical Liturgy, the Bishop washes his hands at this point, thus ceremonially purifying himself for the sacred office which he is about to exercise. The Great Entrance typifies our Lord's going to his Passion and death. Therefore it is customary for the Faithful to do homage to the Holy Gifts at this point, although these are not yet consecrated.

What does the anaphora give thanks for?[2]

This passage gives thanks for creation, restoration after the fall and God’s benefits both known and unknown. It addresses the Father together with the Son and Holy Spirit and places earthly worship alongside the ministry of the angels. Thanksgiving is thus connected with the account of God’s saving work.[2]

Read original passage

Anaphora of Saint John Chrysostom

It is meet and right that we should laud thee, bless thee, praise thee, give thanks unto thee, and adore thee in all places of thy dominion: for thou art God ineffable, incomprehensible, invisible, inconceivable; thou art from everlasting and art changeless, thou, and thine Only-begotten Son, and thy Holy Spirit. Thou from nothingness hast called us into being; and when we had fallen away from thee, thou didst raise us up again; and thou hast not ceased to do all things until thou hadst brought us back to heaven, and hadst endowed us with thy kingdom which is to come. For all which things we give thanks unto thee, and thine Only-begotten Son, and thy Holy Spirit; for all the things whereof we know, and whereof we know not; for all thy benefits bestowed upon us, both manifest and unseen. And we render thanks unto thee for this ministry which thou dost deign to accept at our hands, although before thee stand thousands of Archangels and myriads of Angels, with the Cherubim, and Seraphim, six-winged, many-eyed, who soar aloft, borne on their pinions.

What is the invocation of the Holy Spirit?[2]

An invocation is an appeal or calling upon God. In this passage the prayer asks that the Holy Spirit be sent upon the assembled people and the gifts. The excerpt is part of the printed Eucharistic prayer and retains its own place within that complete order.[2]

Read original passage

Invocation of the Holy Spirit

Again we offer unto thee this reasonable and unbloody service. And we beseech and implore thee, and offer our supplications unto thee, that thou wilt send thy Holy Spirit upon us, and upon these Gifts here spread forth.

The anaphora as a further reading[3]

The linked resource concerns the Eucharistic Canon, also called the anaphora. It offers further explanation of the prayer whose opening thanksgiving and invocation are represented here.[3]
